There are 59 across NYC: 18 in Brooklyn, 14 in Queens, 12 in Manhattan, 12 in the Bronx, and 3 in Staten Island. They vote on issues across policy areas such as land use (first stop in ULURP), landmarks, liquor licenses, transportation, and budgets (past votes and minutes). Members are appointed by the borough president (half) and the city council members overlapping with the community district.
about.p2: CB6 & Beyond covers all 59 community districts in the five boroughs, with Brooklyn Community Board 6 in depth. Pick your board and the whole app follows it: its map, meetings, officials, blocks, parks, streets, land use and health. The NYC tab holds each borough and the city as a whole.
about.p3: Please note that the numbers start over in every borough, so there is a CB6 in Manhattan, Queens, and the Bronx.

boards.intro: New York City has 59 community boards in five boroughs. Tap one for its district: who represents it, its blocks, parks, streets, land use and health, with 311, crime and permits.

items.a: Community boards are the official, independent, and advisory bodies of New York City Government. There are 59 across NYC: 18 in Brooklyn, 14 in Queens, 12 in Manhattan, 12 in the Bronx, and 3 in Staten Island. They vote on issues across policy areas such as land use (first stop in ULURP), landmarks, liquor licenses, transportation, and budgets. Members are appointed by the borough president (half) and the city council members overlapping with the community district.

Type your address or use your location on Home, or tap a seal in the row at the top. The Boards tab lists all 59 with their neighborhoods, borough by borough. The numbers start over in every borough, so there is a CB6 in Manhattan, Queens and the Bronx too.

Every major land use change in a district, from a rezoning to a variance, goes through a public review with fixed steps and clocks, and the board gets a formal vote in each one. The vote is advisory, but it is on the record and the later decision makers read it. Boards also weigh in on liquor licenses, landmarks, transportation and the budget.
items.q: What does a board vote on?

items.a: The next meeting is on Home once you pick a board. The Calendar tab has community board meetings across the city, with a filter for yours.
Tap your board in the Boards tab for its office, phone, website, chair and district manager.
items.q: How do I contact my board?

items.a: Report it to 311 first. If it needs follow up, email the board office: email creates a record the board can follow up on. 311, crime, tickets and permits, under Around you on Home, shows the complaints filed in your district.
items.q: How do I report a problem like a pothole or a missed pickup?

items.a: Who represents your board, under Around you on Home, lists every elected official from the City Council to Congress. Every elected official in the city is in the NYC tab.
Your block on Home, or Block cards under Around you: find your street for alternate side parking, trash and recycling days, your poll site and the nearest subway.
items.q: How do I find alternate side parking, trash days or my poll site for my block?

items.a: Tap the Election 2026 card on Home for your ballot, your early voting site and your Election Day poll site.
Type an address in the box above the map on Home, or press and hold on the map to drop a pin.
items.q: How do I search the map?

items.a: Yes. The maps, lots, blocks and profiles for all five boroughs are on your phone and work without a connection. 311, crime, tickets and permits for your board download the first time you open them and are kept on your phone; CB6's are built in. Typing an address uses the internet when it is available; offline, the search matches the city’s blocks.
items.q: Does the app work without a connection?

items.a: The app checks for new meetings and data whenever it opens with a connection. Pull down on Home to check now; the time of the last check is at the bottom of Home.
Tap Take the tour at the top of How to use CB6 & Beyond.

landmarks.sub: CB6 has 6 historic districts. The Landmarks & Land Use Committee reviews all Certificate of Appropriateness applications before they go to LPC.
landmarks.title: Landmarks & Historic Districts

what.text: An NYC Historic District is a defined area designated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission for its architectural, cultural, or historic significance. Places like large parts of Park Slope and Cobble Hill reflect distinct periods of the city’s history, and exterior changes generally require LPC approval to preserve that character. A good rule of thumb is to check the street signs: brown with white lettering usually means you are in a historic district, while green with white lettering usually means you are not. In Brooklyn Community Board 6, that often means we are part of the review process for applications seeking LPC approval, including Certificates of Appropriateness for proposed changes to landmarked properties.
